What are the steps involved in changing the content displayed in the Properties window when the user changes focus to another window in Visual Studio or selects a different project item in Solution Explorer?

1. The object created by your VSPackage that is sited in the selected window calls QueryService to have STrackSelection invoke ITrackSelection.
  2. The selection container, provided by the selected window, creates its own ISelectionContainer object. When the selection changes, the VSPackage calls ITrackSelection.OnSelectChange to notify any listeners in the environment, including the Properties window, of the change. 
  3. Calling ITrackSelection.OnSelectChange and passing it the selected hierarchy items in the VSHPROPID_BrowseObject parameter populates the ISelectionContainer object.
  4. An object derived from the IDispatch Interface is returned for VSHPROPID_BrowseObject for the item requested, and the environment wraps it into an ISelectionContainer. 
  5. The environment invokes the methods of ISelectionContainer to get the objects based on the IDispatch interface to fill in the Properties window.

6. Click the ellipsis next to Use Runtime to open the Configure Behavior dialog box.
7. Select Customize.

10. Select Update in the Behavior list.
11. Select Customize.
12. Select the UpdateCustomers method in the Customize list.
13. Map the Original_CustomerID method argument to the CustomerID (Original) class property.
14. Click Apply to save the configuration for the selected Class and Behavior.
15. Select Delete in the Behavior list.
16. Select Customize.
17. Select the DeleteCustomers method in the Customize list.
18. Map the Original_CustomerID method argument to the CustomerID (Original) class property.

What is the loop process that IntelliTest follows in Visual Studio to generate inputs?

The steps of the loop are:
    1. IntelliTest determines inputs `i` such that `q(i)=false` using a constraint solver. By construction, the input `i` will take an execution path not seen before.
    2. IntelliTest executes the test with the chosen input `i`, and monitors the execution of the test and the program under test.
    3. During the execution, the program takes a particular path determined by the conditional branches of the program. IntelliTest computes a representation of this predicate.
    4. IntelliTest sets `q := (q or p)`, recording the fact that it has seen the path represented by `p`.
    5. The process returns to step 1.

How can I create a custom SharePoint site column, content type, and list in Visual Studio?

This process involves several steps. 
  1. Add a list to your project. In Solution Explorer, choose the project node. 
  2. On the menu bar, choose Project > Add New Item. 
  3. Either in Visual C# or Visual Basic, expand the SharePoint node. 
  4. In the Templates pane, choose the List template, change its name to Patients, and then choose the Add button.
  5. Leave the Customize the list based on setting as Default (Custom List), and then choose the Finish button. 
  6. In the List Designer, choose the Content Types button to show the Content Type Settings dialog box. 
  7. Choose the new row, choose the Patient Info content type in the list of content types, and then choose the OK button. This adds all of the site columns from the Patient Info content type into the list.
  8. Delete all of the site columns in the list except for specific ones: Patient ID, Patient Name, Home Phone, E-Mail, Doctor Name, and Comments.
  9. Under Column Display Name, choose an empty row, add a custom list column, and name it Hospital. Leave its data type as Single Line of Text.
  10. Check the Required box next to the Patient ID and Patient Name boxes.
  11. On the Views tab, create a view by entering Patient Details in a blank row under the View Name column.
  12. Choose the new Patient Details row, and then choose the Set as Default button.
  13. Add specific columns to the Selected Columns list in this order: Patient ID, Patient Name, Home Phone, E-Mail, Doctor Name, Hospital, Comments.
  14. In the Properties list, choose the Sorting and Grouping property, and then choose the ellipsis button to display the Sorting and Grouping dialog box.
  15. In the Column Name list, choose Patient Name, ensure that the Sorting column is set to Ascending, and then choose the OK button. 

This process will create a custom SharePoint site column, content type, and list in Visual Studio.

How can you target Visual Studio 2022 (ARM64) when creating an extension in Visual Studio 2022?

To target Visual Studio 2022 (ARM64) when creating an extension in Visual Studio 2022, you need to modify the created project as follows: 

For Managed Visual Studio extensions:
1. Open the VSIX project to your solution. This project will target Visual Studio 2022 ARM64.
2. Verify that the VSIX project builds properly. You might need to add references to match your original VSIX project to resolve any compiler errors.
3. Use the package references 17.x (or earlier) in your Visual Studio 2022-targeted project file. Use the NuGet Package Manager or directly edit the project file.      
4. If your project is already built against **Any CPU**, then you do not need to edit the build configuration as it will build for **ARM64** as well. However, if you want to target only **ARM64**, then change your project to build **ARM64** instead of **Any CPU**.
5. Edit your *source.extension.vsixmanifest* file to reflect targeting Visual Studio 2022. Set the `<InstallationTarget>` tag to indicate Visual Studio 2022. Set the `ProductArchitecture` element to indicate an ARM64 payload.

For C++ Visual Studio extensions:
1. Open the VSIX project to your solution. This project will target Visual Studio 2022 ARM64.
2. Verify that the VSIX project builds properly. You might need to add references to match your original VSIX project to resolve any compiler errors.
3. Change your project from building for targeting **ARM64**. 
4. Update dependency - Any dependency that your extension might have on a native module will have to be updated to an ARM64 image.
5. Edit your *source.extension.vsixmanifest* file to reflect targeting Visual Studio 2022. Set the `<InstallationTarget>` tag to indicate Visual Studio 2022. Set the `ProductArchitecture` element to indicate an ARM64 payload.
Path to the document: extensibility/arm64/target-arm64-visual-studio-extension.md#Add-a-Visual-Studio-2022-target:-ARM64

What are the steps to suppress "missing docstring" warnings using a `.pylintrc` file in Visual Studio's Python project?

  1. In Solution Explorer, right-click the project and select Add > Existing Item.
  1. In the dialog, browse to the folder that has the new `.pylintrc` file. Select the `.pylintrc` file, and then select Add.
  1. In Solution Explorer, open the `.pylintrc` file for editing.
  1. Locate the `[MESSAGES CONTROL]` section, and then locate the `disable` setting within that section.
  1. Append the string `,missing-docstring` (including the comma prefix) to the `disable` setting value.
  1. Save the `.pylintrc` file.
  1. Run pylint again. Notice that the "missing docstring" warnings are now suppressed.

    3. The Properties window now displays properties for the form. 
    4. If you don't see Properties, select View > Properties Window.
    5. Find the Text property in the Properties window and enter the value *Picture Viewer*, and then choose Enter.
    6. Select the form, again. Select the form's lower-right drag handle.
    7. Drag the handle to resize the form so the form is wider and a bit taller.
    8. On the left side of the Visual Studio IDE, select the Toolbox tab.
    9. Select the small triangle symbol next to Containers to open the group.
    10. Double-click TableLayoutPanel in the Toolbox.
    11. With the TableLayoutPanel selected, find the Dock property, which has the value None. 
    12. Select the dropdown arrow and then select Fill, which is the large button in the middle of the dropdown menu.
    13. In the form, select the TableLayoutPanel. In the upper-right corner, there's a small black triangle button. Select the triangle to display the control's task list.
    14. Select Edit Rows and Columns to display the Column and Row Styles dialog box.
    15. Select Column1 and set its size to 15 percent. Be sure the Percent option is selected.
    16. Select Column2 and set it to 85 percent.
    17. From Show at the top of the Column and Row Styles dialog box, select Rows. Set Row1 to 90 percent and Row2 to 10 percent. Select OK to save your changes.

Can you provide a step-by-step guide on how to set a breakpoint condition in Visual Studio for a scenario where we want to pause when the value of a variable exceeds a certain number?

Yes, here are the steps to define a breakpoint condition on a `for` loop statement so the Debugger pauses only when the value of the `i` variable exceeds 1600:
   1. To set the breakpoint condition, right-click the red breakpoint dot and select Conditions or use the keyboard shortcut Alt+F9 > C.
   2. In the Breakpoint Settings popup dialog, configure the following settings to create the Condition:
        1. Set the condition type to Conditional Expression.
        2. Define the condition evaluation to Is true.
        3. Enter `i > 1600` as the condition value.
        4. Select Close.
   3. Select F5 to continue debugging and program execution. Observe that the program runs many iterations before it reaches the conditional breakpoint. 
   4. You can confirm that the Debugger correctly pauses program execution when it reaches the conditional breakpoint. When the condition is met, the Locals window shows the `i` variable value as `1608`.
   5. To run the program to completion, you can disable the breakpoint and continue the program execution. To disable the breakpoint, hover over the red dot and select Disable, or right-click the red dot and select Disable breakpoint. Then select Continue (or press F5) to run the program.

How can a grayscale texture shader be implemented in Visual Studio using the Shader Designer?

A grayscale texture shader can be implemented by modifying the color value of a texture sample before you write it to the final output color. The steps are as follows:

  2. Disconnect the RGB terminal of the Texture Sample node from the RGB terminal of the Final Color node. This makes room for the node that's added in the next step.
  3. Add a Desaturate node to the graph. 
  4. Calculate the grayscale value by using the Desaturate node. 
  5. Connect the grayscale color value to the final color by moving the Output terminal of the Desaturate node to the RGB terminal of the Final Color node.

Based on the information contained in the project section of the `.sln` file, the environment loads each project file. What are the three ways in which the Session Debug Manager in Visual Studio attempts to attach to the program being debugged?

   1. For programs that are launched by the debug engine through the LaunchSuspended method, the SDM tries to obtain the IDebugProgramNodeAttach2 interface from the IDebugProgramNode2 object associated with the program being attached to. If the SDM can obtain the IDebugProgramNodeAttach2 interface, it then calls the OnAttach method.
   2. If the SDM can obtain the IDebugProgramEx2 interface from the program being attached to, it calls the Attach method. This approach is typical for programs that were launched remotely by the port supplier.
   3. If the program cannot be attached through the IDebugProgramNodeAttach2::OnAttach or IDebugProgramEx2::Attach methods, the SDM loads the debug engine (if not already loaded) by calling the CoCreateInstance function and then calls the Attach method. What are the best practices to follow when authoring a custom target in Visual Studio?

   1. Use the `DependsOnTargets` attribute to specify targets that you require to be completed before your target executes. For a chain of targets you control, each target can specify the previous member of the chain in `DependsOnTargets`.
   2. Use `BeforeTargets` for any target that you do not control that you must execute before, like `BeforeTargets="PrepareForBuild"` for a target that needs to run early in the build.
   3. Use `AfterTargets` for any target that you do not control that guarantees the outputs you need are available, such as `AfterTargets="ResolveReferences"` for something that will modify a list of references.
   4. These attributes can be used in combination, for example, `DependsOnTargets="GenerateAssemblyInfo" BeforeTargets="BeforeCompile"`.

What are the steps to re-sign the application and deployment manifests with Mage.exe in Visual Studio?

    2. Change directories to the folder that contains the manifest files that you want to sign.
    3. Type the following command to sign the application manifest file. Replace ManifestFileName with the name of your manifest file plus the extension. Replace Certificate with the relative or fully qualified path of the certificate file and replace Password with the password for the certificate.
    ```cmd
    mage -sign ManifestFileName.manifest -CertFile Certificate -Password Password
    ```
    4. Type the following command to update and sign the deployment manifest file, replacing the placeholder names as in the previous step.
    ```cmd
    mage -update DeploymentManifest -appmanifest ApplicationManifest -CertFile Certificate -Password Password
    ```
    5. Optionally, copy the master deployment manifest (publish\<appname>.application) to your version deployment directory (publish\Application Files\<appname>_<version>).

    1. Launch Visual Studio and select **File** > **New** > **Project**.
    2. In the **Create a new project** dialog, search for _python_, and select the **From Existing Python code** template, and select **Next**.
    3. In the **Configure your new project** dialog, enter a project **Name** and **Location**, choose the solution to contain the project, and select **Create**.
    4. In the **Create New Project from Existing Python Code** wizard, set the **Folder path** to your existing code, set a **Filter** for file types, and specify any **Search paths** that your project requires, then select **Next**. If you don't know the search paths, leave the field blank.
    5. On the next page, select the **Startup file** for your project. Visual Studio selects the default global Python interpreter and version. You can change the environment by using the dropdown menu. When you're ready, select **Next**.
    6. Select the location to store the project file (a _.pyproj_ file on disk). If applicable, you can also include autodetection of virtual environments and customize the project for different web frameworks. If you're unsure of these options, leave the fields set to the defaults.
    7. Select **Finish**.
    8. To set a different startup file, locate the file in **Solution Explorer**, right-click the file, and select **Set as Startup File**.

Remember, this process doesn't move or copy any original source files. If you want to work with a copy of your files, first duplicate the folder and then create the project.

How can I troubleshoot the issue where Visual Studio can't create a manifest file for a diagsession?

You can troubleshoot this issue by providing additional logging information. From an elevated command prompt, run the following commands to enable logging:

```console
reg add HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\VisualStudio\DiagnosticsHub /v LogLevel /t REG_SZ /d All /reg:32
reg add HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\VisualStudio\DiagnosticsHub /v LogDirectory /t REG_SZ /d [directory of your choice] /reg:32
```

Start Visual Studio, reproduce your scenario, close Visual Studio, then zip up your chosen DiagnosticsHub log directory and attach it to the ticket. After adding the log to your ticket, run these commands to disable logging:

```console
reg delete HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\VisualStudio\DiagnosticsHub /f /v LogLevel /reg:32
reg delete HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\Microsoft\VisualStudio\DiagnosticsHub /f /v LogDirectory /reg:32
```

If I suspect a race condition error in my Visual Studio build process, what are the steps I can take to diagnose and fix it?

If you suspect a race condition error, you can follow these steps:
1. Check if any other program is using those files.
2. Try running builds with the MSBuild `/m:1` option and see if the problem persists.
3. Generate a log with the verbosity set to `Normal` or greater, and view it with the Structured Log Viewer.
4. Search the log for the filename of the file that triggers the failure and find all places where it is used.
5. Note the property settings in effect for each instance of the project's build and compare them.
6. Search the project files for `ProjectReference` where the `Include` attribute specifies that project. Look for differences in metadata.
7. Consider the meaning of property settings that are different and decide whether they need to be different or not. Fix the problem accordingly.
8. If the error is in an SDK not under your control, report the issue to the SDK owner.

  - Commands, submenus, and groups can be assigned to one parenting group or menu using the parent field of their defining directive. 
  - A command table can't be organized solely through the parent fields in the directives as they can only take one parent argument.

  <UsingTask

  <ItemGroup>

  1. Open the Administrative Tools window by clicking Start and then choose Control Panel. Choose Switch to Classic View in Control Panel and then double-click Administrative Tools.
  2. In Administrative Tools, double-click Internet Information Services (IIS) Manager.
  3. In the Connections pane, expand the <computer name> node if necessary.
  4. Under the <computer name> node, click Application Pools.
  5. In the Application Pools list, right-click the name of the pool your application runs in and then click Advanced Settings.
  6. In the Advanced Settings dialog box, locate the Process Model section, and perform either set Ping Enabled to False or set Ping Maximum Response Time to a value larger than 90 seconds.

How do I publish my project to Azure App Service from Visual Studio 2017 and later versions?

To publish your project to Azure App Service from Visual Studio 2017 and later versions, follow these steps:

    1. In Visual Studio Solution Explorer, right-click the project and select Add > New Item. Choose the Azure web.config (Fast CGI) template, and select Add. This creates a `web.config` file in your project root.
    2. Modify the `PythonHandler` entry in the `web.config` file so the path matches the Python installation on the server.
    3. Set the `WSGI_HANDLER` entry in the `web.config` file as appropriate for the framework you're using.
    4. For Django apps, add the URL domain or IP address to the `ALLOWED_HOSTS` entry in the `settings.py` file.
    5. Select the template by going to Solution Explorer, expanding your project folder, right-clicking the static folder, and selecting Add > New Item. Then, select the Azure Static files web.config template and select Add.
    6. Save your project in Solution Explorer, then right-click your project and select Publish.
    7. In the Publish window, specify the publishing target. Select Azure for the Target and Azure App Service (Windows) for the Specific target. Choose the appropriate App Service for your subscription.
    8. After the publish creation process completes, select Close.
    9. When you see the "Ready to publish" message for the web app, select Publish.
    10. When publishing succeeds, the default browser opens on the site URL.

If the site URL doesn't automatically open, select Open site to view the web app in the browser.

How can I write unit tests for C++ DLLs using Visual Studio?

You can write unit tests for C++ DLLs using Visual Studio by following these steps:
   1. Create a native test project. The test project is located in the same solution as the DLL project.
   2. Create a DLL project. This walkthrough creates a new DLL, but the procedure for testing an existing DLL is similar.
   3. Make the DLL functions visible to the tests.
   4. Iteratively augment the tests. We recommend a "red-green-refactor" cycle, in which development of the code is led by the tests.
   5. Debug failing tests. You can run tests in debug mode.
   6. Refactor while keeping the tests unchanged. Refactoring means improving the structure of the code without changing its external behavior. You do not change the tests while making a refactoring change to the code. The tests help make sure that you do not introduce bugs while you are refactoring.
   7. Check coverage. Unit tests are more useful when they exercise more of your code. You can discover which parts of your code have been used by the tests.
   8. Isolate units from external resources. Typically, a DLL is dependent on other components of the system that you are developing, such as other DLLs, databases, or remote subsystems. It is useful to test each unit in isolation from its dependencies. External components can make tests run slowly. During development, the other components might not be complete.

What are the steps that occur when you create a SharePoint package (*.wsp*) in Visual Studio?

    1. The Features and packages are validated to ensure that the physical and semantic structure of the package is correct.
    2. The Features, project items, and package files in the package are enumerated. Manifest files for packages and Features are transformed to include all necessary information for deployment and activation. The tokens are replaced with the fully qualified value.

Could you explain the process of how a watch list expression is evaluated in Visual Studio?

The process of evaluating a watch list expression in Visual Studio involves several steps: 
   1. Visual Studio calls the DE's GetExpressionContext to get an expression context that can be used to evaluate expressions.
   2. For each expression in the watch list, Visual Studio calls ParseText to convert the expression text into a parsed expression.
   3. IDebugExpressionContext2::ParseText calls Parse to do the actual work of parsing the text and produce an IDebugParsedExpression object.
   4. IDebugExpressionContext2::ParseText creates an IDebugExpression2 object and puts the IDebugParsedExpression object into it. This IDebugExpression2 object is then returned to Visual Studio.
   5. Visual Studio calls EvaluateSync to evaluate the parsed expression.
   6. IDebugExpression2::EvaluateSync passes the call to EvaluateSync to do the actual evaluation and produce an IDebugProperty2 object that is returned to Visual Studio.
   7. Visual Studio calls GetPropertyInfo to obtain the value of the expression that is then displayed in the watch list.

How can I use a custom image for the command icon in Visual Studio?

You can add custom images by following these steps:
1. Rename the image source files to follow the `%Custom Moniker%.*` pattern (for example, *MyImage.1.png*). Files prefixed with the same moniker will all be used as backing sources for the same custom moniker. Different source will be used based on the requested icon size.
    - For example, *MyImage.16.16.png* (a 16\*16 png), *MyImage.20.20.png* (a 20\*20 png) and *MyImage.xaml* are all considered as sources for `MyImage`.
    - When the requested icon size is 16*16, *MyImage.16.16.png* will be used, when requested size is 20\*20, *MyImage.20.20.png* will be used, in all other cases, *MyImage.xaml* will be used.
2. Put all of the image source files under `Images` folder. The default image assets folder is `Images`, but you can also customize it by adding `<ImageAssetsPath>%YourFolder%</ImageAssetsPath>`

Can you explain some best practices when dealing with an ITextDocumentSnapshot in Visual Studio?

You can use the indexer syntax, `textDocument[0]`, to read character by character in the document without copying it to a string. If you need to create a string, use the overload that takes a `Span`, to avoid creating a large throwaway string. Additionally, don't assume that lines or documents will be short. Remember that ITextDocumentSnapshot references large data structures that may consume memory if an old version is stored. The best practice is to update positions and spans that you're storing long term to the latest document version so the old ITextDocumentSnapshot version can be garbage collected.

What sequence of methods and events does the session debug manager (SDM) call in Visual Studio to attach the debugger to a program?

Otherwise, the Attach method is called to complete the attach process. If S_OK is returned, the DE is to be loaded in the same process as the SDM. The SDM then performs the following tasks: 1) Calls GetEngineInfo to get the engine information of the DE. 2) Co-creates the DE. 3) Calls Attach. What is the process by which Visual Studio retrieves locals for a method from the expression evaluator?

The process begins when Visual Studio calls the debug engine's GetDebugProperty to get an IDebugProperty2 object that represents all the properties of the stack frame, including the locals. This object then calls GetMethodProperty to get an object describing the method in which the breakpoint occurred. It then calls GetContainerField with the supplied IDebugAddress object to get an IDebugContainerField that represents the method containing the specified address. The IDebugContainerField interface is queried for the IDebugMethodField interface which gives access to the method's locals. Then, GetMethodProperty instantiates a class that runs the IDebugProperty2 interface to represent the method's locals. The IDebugMethodField object, along with other objects, are placed in this class. When the class object is initialized, GetInfo is called on the IDebugMethodField object to get a FIELD_INFO structure that contains all displayable information about the method itself. The GetMethodProperty then returns the class object as an IDebugProperty2 object. Visual Studio then calls EnumChildren on the returned IDebugProperty2 object which returns an object containing the method's locals. Finally, Visual Studio calls Next to obtain a structure for each local, followed by GetPropertyInfo for each local to obtain its name, value, and type.
Path to the document: extensibility/debugger/sample-implementation-of-locals.md#In-this-section

How does Visual Studio get the locals for a method from the expression evaluator?

Visual Studio obtains locals for a method from the expression evaluator through the following steps:
    1. Visual Studio calls the debug engine's GetDebugProperty to get an IDebugProperty2 object that represents all the properties of the stack frame, including the locals.
    2. IDebugStackFrame2::GetDebugProperty calls GetMethodProperty to get an object that describes the method within which the breakpoint happened.
    3. IDebugExpressionEvaluator::GetMethodProperty calls GetContainerField with the supplied IDebugAddress object to get an IDebugContainerField that represents the method containing the specified address.
    4. The IDebugContainerField interface is queried for the IDebugMethodField interface that gives access to the method's locals.
    5. IDebugExpressionEvaluator::GetMethodProperty instantiates a class (CFieldProperty in the sample) that runs the IDebugProperty2 interface to represent the method's locals.
    6. When the CFieldProperty object is initialized, GetInfo is called on the IDebugMethodField object to get a FIELD_INFO structure.
    7. IDebugExpressionEvaluator::GetMethodProperty returns the CFieldProperty object as an IDebugProperty2 object.
    8. Visual Studio calls EnumChildren on the returned IDebugProperty2 object.
    9. Visual Studio calls Next to obtain a DEBUG_PROPERTY_INFO structure for each local.
    10. Visual Studio calls GetPropertyInfo for each local to obtain the local's name, value, and type.
Path to the document: extensibility/debugger/sample-implementation-of-locals.md#Related-sections

Can you describe the steps to create basic Phong shaders in Visual Studio using the Shader Designer?

3. Add an Add node to the graph. In the Toolbox, under Math, select Add and move it to the design surface.
4. Add a Specular node to the graph. In the Toolbox, under Utility, select Specular and move it to the design surface.
5. Add the specular contribution by moving the Output terminal of the Specular node to the X terminal of the Add node, and then moving the Output terminal of the Lambert node to the Y terminal of the Add node. This combines the total diffuse and specular color contributions for the pixel.
6. Connect the computed color value to the final color by moving the Output terminal of the Add node to the RGB terminal of the Final Color node.

How does Visual Studio IDE locate the source control plug-in DLL?

The Visual Studio IDE can locate the source control plug-in DLL in two ways. One way is to find the default source control plug-in and connect to it silently. The IDE does this by looking under the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\SourceCodeControlProvider subkey for the entry ProviderRegKey. The value of this entry points to another subkey. The IDE then looks for an entry named SccServerPath in that second subkey under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE. The value of this entry points the IDE to the DLL. The second way is to find all registered source control plug-ins, from which the user can choose. The IDE looks under the HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\Software\SourceCodeControlProvider\InstalledSCCProviders subkey for all entries. Each entry has a name and a value. The IDE displays a list of these names to the user. When a user chooses a name, the IDE finds the value for the selected name that points to a subkey. The IDE then looks for an entry named SccServerPath in that subkey under HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE. The value of that entry points the IDE to the correct DLL.

What does the following code example in Visual Studio do with the CombinePath task?
```xml
  <PropertyGroup>
    <OutputType>Exe</OutputType>
    <TargetFramework>netcoreapp3.1</TargetFramework>
    <PublishRoot>C:\Site1\</PublishRoot>
    <ReleaseDirectory>Release\</ReleaseDirectory>
  </PropertyGroup>

  <ItemGroup>
    <LangDirectories Include="en-us\;fr-fr\"/>
  </ItemGroup>

  <Target Name="CreateOutputDirectories" AfterTargets="Build">
    <CombinePath BasePath="$(PublishRoot)$(ReleaseDirectory)" Paths="@(LangDirectories)" >
      <Output TaskParameter="CombinedPaths" ItemName="OutputDirectories"/>
    </CombinePath>
    <MakeDir Directories="@(OutputDirectories)" />
  </Target>
```

The code example creates a target named "CreateOutputDirectories" which runs after the "Build" target. It then uses the CombinePath task to combine the base path, which is a concatenation of the values of the `PublishRoot` and `ReleaseDirectory` properties, with the paths specified in the `LangDirectories` item list. The combined paths are then assigned to the `OutputDirectories` item list. The `MakeDir` task is then used to create directories at each of these combined paths.

How does Visual Studio obtain the locals for a method from the expression evaluator?

Here are the steps that Visual Studio follows:
    1. Visual Studio calls the debug engine's GetDebugProperty to get an IDebugProperty2 object.
    2. IDebugStackFrame2::GetDebugProperty calls GetMethodProperty to get an object describing the method within which the breakpoint happened.
    3. IDebugExpressionEvaluator::GetMethodProperty calls GetContainerField with the supplied IDebugAddress object.
    4. The IDebugContainerField interface is queried for the IDebugMethodField interface.
    5. IDebugExpressionEvaluator::GetMethodProperty instantiates a class (CFieldProperty in the sample) that runs the IDebugProperty2 interface.
    6. When the CFieldProperty object is initialized, GetInfo is called on the IDebugMethodField object.
    7. IDebugExpressionEvaluator::GetMethodProperty returns the CFieldProperty object as an IDebugProperty2 object.
    8. Visual Studio calls EnumChildren on the returned IDebugProperty2 object with the filter guidFilterLocalsPlusArgs.
    9. Visual Studio calls Next to obtain a DEBUG_PROPERTY_INFO structure for each local.
    10. Visual Studio calls GetPropertyInfo for each local to obtain the local's name, value, and type. This information is displayed in the Locals window.

What are the three formats I can export a shader in from the Shader Designer in Visual Studio, and what are the implications of each?

The three formats are HLSL Pixel Shader (.hlsl), Compiled Pixel Shader (.cso), and C++ Header (.h). The HLSL Pixel Shader allows you to modify the shader later and is easier to debug and patch based on end-user problems but may increase load time and be easier for users to modify. The Compiled Pixel Shader is also modifiable and offers easier debugging and patching. However, it does not incur extra runtime overhead when the shader is loaded by the app, but skilled users can still modify it. The C++ Header exports the shader as a byte array containing HLSL bytecode. It's more difficult to debug and patch, and the app must be recompiled to test the fix, but it's harder for users to modify.

What does the Duplication Factor indicate in the File IO report in Visual Studio?

The Duplication Factor for an individual file read is the number of bytes read from the file divided by the size of the file. For an aggregate read, it's the total number of bytes read from the file divided by the average size of the file across all read operations. This indicates if you're reading or writing more than what you need to from the file. If you have a duplication factor of 3x, that means you are reading from the file is 3 times the size of the file itself, which may be an indication that you're reading and processing more than you realized. How can you clone a GitHub repository of Python code using Visual Studio?

   1. In Visual Studio, select **Git** > **Clone**.
   1. In the **Clone a repository** dialog, specify the GitHub repository to clone:
        1. For the **Repository location**, enter the URL of the repository to clone. For example, `https://github.com/gregmalcolm/python_koans`.
        1. For the **Path**, enter the folder on your system where you want Visual Studio to store the cloned files. Visual Studio doesn't automatically create a new subfolder with the name of the repository.
        1. When you're ready, select **Clone**.
   After cloning completes, Visual Studio opens the **Git Changes** pane for the repository and you can see the folder with the cloned repository files in **Solution Explorer**.
   1. Select **Git** > **Local Repositories** to confirm the cloned repository is now in the list.

Please note that in the quickstart, a direct clone of the _python\_koans_ repository on GitHub is created. This repository is protected by its author from direct changes, so attempting to commit changes to the repository fails.
